summary: Defines two new Mobile IP extensions that let equipment vendors and organizations add their own vendor or organization specific data. They are meant for research or deployment uses the standard does not cover.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IP messages have a fixed set of fields, and no room for a vendor to add its own. This RFC defines two optional blocks that can be added to those messages, so a vendor or organization can carry its own data. One of them is critical: if the receiver does not understand it, the whole message is thrown away.

subtitle: Two Mobile IP extensions that let vendors and organizations carry their own private data in Mobile IP messages.

tldr.problem: The Mobile IP specification has no room for an organization or a vendor to put its own information into a Mobile IP message, and wide-scale deployment of Mobile IP made that a practical need.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two optional extension blocks: a Critical one, CVSE, whose type number is 38, and a Normal one, NVSE, whose type number is 134. Each carries a vendor identifier, a vendor-specific type and a vendor-specific value.
tldr.outcome: A vendor can attach its own data to a registration, and the receiver decides what to do with it. An unrecognised Critical extension causes the whole message to be discarded, while an unrecognised Normal extension is skipped. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3025.

today: RFC 3115 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2001. It obsoletes RFC 3025, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Vendor Extensions Were Needed
sections.content:
The current specification of Mobile IP (RFC 2002) does not allow organizations and vendors to include organization or vendor-specific information in Mobile IP messages. With the imminent wide-scale deployment of Mobile IP, the RFC says it is useful to have vendor or organization-specific extensions to support this capability. The document defines two extensions that vendors and organizations can use for their own specific purposes, for research or deployment.

The RFC also defines the term silently discard. An implementation that silently discards a datagram does so without further processing and without indicating an error to the sender. The implementation SHOULD provide the capability of logging the error, including the contents of the discarded datagram, and SHOULD record the event in a statistics counter.

The RFC Editor's note at the top of the document explains why it exists. It corrects discrepancies between the values assigned for CVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and NVSE-TYPE-NUMBER in RFC 3025 and in the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority's repository. In RFC 3025 the CVSE type number was 37 and the NVSE type number was 133, while in the IANA registry under Mobile IP numbers they are 38 and 134. The note says the memo obsoletes RFC 3025, since the current implementations follow the IANA assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP messages have a fixed set of fields, and no room for a vendor to add its own. This RFC defines two optional blocks that can be added to those messages, so a vendor or organization can carry its own data. One of them is critical: if the receiver does not understand it, the whole message is thrown away.

sections.title: The Two Extension Formats
sections.content:
Two Vendor/Organization Specific Extensions are described, the Critical (CVSE) and the Normal (NVSE). The basic differences are that when a Critical extension is encountered but not recognized, the message containing it MUST be silently discarded, whereas when a Normal extension is encountered but not recognized the extension SHOULD be ignored but the rest of the extensions and message data MUST still be processed. The second difference is that the Critical extension has a length field of two octets and the NVSE a length field of only one octet.

The Critical Vendor/Organization Specific Extension has four fields before the data. Type is the value 38. Reserved is reserved for future use, MUST be set to 0 on sending and MUST be ignored on reception. Length is the length in bytes of this extension, not including the Type and Length bytes. Vendor/Org-ID has a high-order octet of 0 and the low-order three octets are the SMI Network Management Private Enterprise Code of the vendor, in network byte order, as defined in the Assigned Numbers RFC (RFC 1700).

After those comes Vendor-CVSE-Type, a 16-bit value indicating the particular type of Vendor-CVSE-Extension, whose administration is done by the vendor, and Vendor-CVSE-Value, the vendor or organization specific data, which is zero or more octets and whose length can be computed from the Length field value. The RFC notes that if an implementation does not recognize the CVSE, according to RFC 2002 the entire packet is to be silently dropped.

The Normal Vendor/Organization Specific Extension has the same shape with two differences. Type is the value 134, and Length is one octet rather than two, with the Reserved field taking the two octets that the length field occupies in the Critical extension. The Vendor/Org-ID is formed the same way, and Vendor-NVSE-Type and Vendor-NVSE-Value play the same roles as their Critical counterparts, with the administration of the types done by the vendor.
sections.plainLanguage: Both blocks start with a type number and a length, then a vendor code and a type number of the vendor's own choosing, then the data. The critical block has a two-byte length field and the normal one a single byte, so the critical block can carry more data.

sections.title: How Extensions Are Processed
sections.content:
Section 2.3 of the RFC gives the processing rules, and they differ between the two extension types.

When a Mobile IP entity receives a registration request message, or any other request or update message, with an extension of type CVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and recognizes it, but the extension contains an unknown or unsupported vendor ID or Vendor-CVSE-Type, a registration reject, or the appropriate deny message, MUST be sent with the error code indicating that the registration was rejected because of the presence of an unknown CVSE.

When the entity receives a registration reply, or any other Mobile IP reply or acknowledgement message, with an extension of type CVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and recognizes it, but the extension contains an unknown or unsupported vendor ID or Vendor-CVSE-Type, the processing depends on the entity's role. If the entity is a transit node for the reply, that is, it processes the registration reply and sends it to another entity, a registration reject MUST be sent with the error code for an unknown CVSE. The RFC's example is that a foreign agent receiving an unknown CVSE in a registration reply from the home agent should send a registration reject to the mobile node. If the entity is not a transit node for the reply, the reply is treated as a reject because of the presence of an unknown CVSE.

The RFC adds a caution for designers: while designing enhancements in which a CVSE is included in a reply message, it should be noted that the reply message could be discarded by the Mobile IP entity processing it. Enhancements that include a CVSE should take that into account.

When a Mobile IP entity receives a Mobile IP related message, such as a registration request or reply or an advertisement or solicitation, with an extension of type NVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and recognizes it, but the extension contains an unknown or unsupported vendor ID or Vendor-NVSE-Type, the entire extension is skipped.

The RFC notes that according to RFC 2002, when an extension numbered within the range 0 through 127 is encountered in a registration message but not recognized, the message containing that extension MUST be silently discarded. It states that the document is compliant with that specification, and specifies the action for the case where the extension type is CVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and is recognized but the vendor ID or the vendor type within it is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: What happens depends on whether the receiver understands the block. If it recognises the block type but not the vendor or the vendor's own type, then in a request it must reject the registration, and in a reply it must either reject it or pass a rejection back. A normal block with an unknown vendor is simply skipped, and the rest of the message is processed as usual.

sections.title: New Error Codes
sections.content:
Section 2.4 defines four error codes, in two pairs.

Registration denied by the Foreign Agent. ERROR-FA-1, code 100: unsupported Vendor-ID, or unable to interpret the Vendor-CVSE-Type, in the CVSE sent by the Mobile Node to the Foreign Agent. ERROR-FA-2, code 101: unsupported Vendor-ID, or unable to interpret the Vendor-CVSE-Type, in the CVSE sent by the Home Agent to the Foreign Agent.

Registration denied by the Home Agent. ERROR-HA-1, code 140: unsupported Vendor-ID, or unable to interpret the Vendor-CVSE-Type, in the CVSE sent by the Mobile Node to the Home Agent. ERROR-HA-2, code 141: unsupported Vendor-ID, or unable to interpret the Vendor-CVSE-Type, in the CVSE sent by the Foreign Agent to the Home Agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Four new error codes say why a registration was rejected. Two are for the foreign agent and two for the home agent, and each pair covers a CVSE that came from the mobile node and one that came from the other agent.

sections.title: Restrictions on Placement
sections.content: Section 3 of the RFC states the restrictions on how these extensions may be used. Multiple TLVs with the types CVSE-TYPE-NUMBER and NVSE-TYPE-NUMBER can be included in a message. TLVs of those two types can be placed anywhere after the fixed portion of the Mobile IP message. These TLVs are expected to be protected by the corresponding authenticator as necessary, and their ordering should not be modified by intermediate nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: More than one of these blocks can appear in a message, and they can go anywhere after the fixed part of the message. The order is not to be changed by any node in the middle, and they are expected to be covered by the message's authenticator.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The Critical Vendor/Organization Specific Extension defined in Section 2.1 and the Normal Vendor/Organization Specific Extension defined in Section 2.2 are new extensions to the Mobile IP protocol, which is defined in RFC 2002 and extended in RFC 2356.

IANA has assigned a Type value for the CVSE and a Type value for the NVSE, taken from the numbering space defined for Mobile IP registration extensions. IANA has also assigned new Foreign Agent error codes, ERROR-FA-1 and ERROR-FA-2, taken from the numbering space defined for Mobile IP Foreign Agent error codes, and new Home Agent error codes, ERROR-HA-1 and ERROR-HA-2, taken from the numbering space defined for Mobile IP Home Agent error codes.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA assigned the type numbers and the four error codes. The RFC also notes that it exists to correct a mismatch: the numbers in the earlier version of this document did not match the ones in the IANA registry, and the implementations followed the registry.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it assumes the Mobile IP messages are authenticated using a method defined by the Mobile IP protocol. It imposes no additional requirements on Mobile IP messages from a security point of view, and says this is not expected to be a security issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assumes the Mobile IP messages are already authenticated by the Mobile IP protocol itself, and adds no further security requirements of its own.
